title: Question 7
stem:
A varying current $I$ passes through a resistor of resistance $R$ in the circuit shown in Fig. 7.1.
{{figure:figure_7_1}}
Fig. 7.1
Fig. 7.2 shows the variation with time $t$ of $I$.
{{figure:figure_7_2}}
Fig. 7.2
The current has magnitude $2I_0$ when it is in the positive direction and $I_0$ when it is in the negative direction. The period of the variation of the current is $T$.

parts.label: (a)(i)
parts.part_stem: Determine expressions, in terms of $I_0$ and $R$, for the power $P$ dissipated in the resistor for the times when:
parts.text: the current is in the negative direction
hints: Hint 1: Think about which formula for heating power in a resistor uses current and resistance, and remember that only the size of the current matters for heating, not whether it is labelled positive or negative.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Heating Power Depends on $I^2$**
When current flows in a resistor, electrical energy is converted to heat. The power is given by $$P = I^2 R$$ The square is important. It means a negative current still gives positive heating power.

Step 2: **Insert the Magnitude $I_0$**
In the negative direction the magnitude is $I_0$. So $$P = (-I_0)^2 R = I_0^2 R$$

parts.text: the current is in the positive direction.
hints: Hint 1: Use the same heating law as before, but now look carefully at Fig. 7.2 to see what the current value is when the trace is above the zero line.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Use the Same Law With Larger Current**
Heating power is still $$P = I^2 R$$ From Fig. 7.2, when the current is in the positive direction, $I = 2I_0$.

Step 2: **Square the Whole Current**
Be careful to square everything, including the 2: $$P = (2I_0)^2 R = 4I_0^2 R$$ Doubling the current gives four times the power.

parts.label: (b)

markscheme_points.text: sketch: square wave of period $T$, with $P$ always non-zero
horizontal lines, from 0 to $0.5T$ and from $1.0T$ to $1.5T$, all at the same level that the scale indicates to be $I_0^2 R$
horizontal lines, from $0.5T$ to $1.0T$ and from $1.5T$ to $2.0T$, at a level that is four times higher than the lower lines

hints: Hint 1: Start by thinking about whether the power graph can ever go negative or follow the up-down shape of the current graph in Fig. 7.2.
Hint 2: Next, match each time interval in Fig. 7.2 to one of your two power values from part (a), keeping the same switching times at $0.5T$, $1.0T$ and $1.5T$.
Hint 3: Finally, think about how to label the $P$-axis so the lower level is $I_0^2R$ and the upper level shows clearly that it is four times larger.
parts.proper_answer: Square wave of period $T$ with $P>0$ at all times. $P = I_0^2R$ from $0$ to $0.5T$ and $1.0T$ to $1.5T$; $P = 4I_0^2R$ from $0.5T$ to $1.0T$ and $1.5T$ to $2.0T$. Upper level four times the lower level.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Power Never Goes Negative**
Current changes sign, but power does not. Because $P = I^2R$, squaring removes the minus sign. So your $P$ against $t$ graph stays fully above zero. It will also be flat-topped because $I$ is constant in each interval.

Step 2: **Build the Low and High Levels**
From $t = 0$ to $0.5T$, $I = -I_0$, so $$P = I_0^2 R$$ From $t = 0.5T$ to $1.0T$, $I = +2I_0$, so $$P = 4I_0^2 R$$ The pattern then repeats: low from $1.0T$ to $1.5T$, high from $1.5T$ to $2.0T$.

Step 3: **Draw and Label to Scale**
Draw horizontal lines with sharp vertical jumps at $0.5T$, $1.0T$ and $1.5T$. Label the $P$-axis with $I_0^2R$ for the lower level and $4I_0^2R$ for the upper level, so the upper line is four times as high as the lower line. The period of the power variation is still $T$.

parts.label: (c)(i)
parts.part_stem: Use your answer in (b) to determine an expression, in terms of $I_0$ and $R$, for:
parts.text: the mean power $\langle P \rangle$ in the resistor
hints: Hint 1: Look at one full period $T$ in your power graph and think about how to average two equal-length blocks, one at $I_0^2R$ for half the time and one at $4I_0^2R$ for half the time.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Average Over One Period**
Mean power is the area under the $P$-$t$ graph for one period divided by the period. In time $T$, the resistor spends $T/2$ at $I_0^2R$ and $T/2$ at $4I_0^2R$.

Step 2: **Calculate the Simple Average**
$$\langle P \rangle = \frac{1}{2}(I_0^2R) + \frac{1}{2}(4I_0^2R) = \frac{5}{2}I_0^2R$$ This is $2.5I_0^2R$, halfway between 1 and 4 in units of $I_0^2R$.

enrichment.label: (c)(i)
key_concepts: equal time spent at two power levels
hints: Hint 1: Look at one full period $T$ in your power graph and think about how to average two equal-length blocks, one at $I_0^2R$ for half the time and one at $4I_0^2R$ for half the time.

parts.label: (c)(ii)
parts.text: the root-mean-square (r.m.s.) current $I_{\text{r.m.s.}}$ in the resistor.
hints: Hint 1: Recall the meaning of r.m.s. current: it is the steady d.c. current that would give the same mean heating power, so start from $\langle P \rangle = I_{r.m.s.}^2 R$.
Hint 2: Now equate that expression to your mean power $\frac{5}{2}I_0^2R$ from (c)(i) and solve for $I_{r.m.s.}$ by cancelling $R$ and taking the square root.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Link Mean Power to R.M.S. Current**
By definition, the r.m.s. current is the equivalent constant current that produces the same mean power: $$\langle P \rangle = I_{r.m.s.}^2 R$$

Step 2: **Equate and Solve**
Insert the mean power from (c)(i): $$I_{r.m.s.}^2 R = \frac{5}{2}I_0^2 R$$ Cancel $R$ and take the square root: $$I_{r.m.s.} = \sqrt{\frac{5}{2}}I_0$$ Notice this is larger than $I_0$ but smaller than $2I_0$, as you would expect for an average of the two levels.

key_concepts: equivalent d.c. current for same heating
